sections.overview: Caenorhabditis elegans is a tiny, transparent free-living nematode and a major laboratory model for development, genetics, neurons and ageing.
sections.identification: Adults are about a millimetre long; most are self-fertilizing hermaphrodites, while rare males have a specialized mating tail.
sections.habitat: In nature it is often found in moist, bacteria-rich rotting plant matter such as compost or decaying fruit, not simply as a permanent soil dweller.
sections.diet: It eats bacteria, including Escherichia coli in laboratory culture; food supply and crowding can alter development.
sections.behavior: When food is depleted or conditions crowded, larvae can enter the stress-resistant dauer stage, survive for months and disperse.
sections.reproduction: At 25 °C its egg-to-egg cycle can take about three days; hermaphrodites self-fertilize, although males permit outcrossing.
sections.ecology: It is one of many Caenorhabditis species; relatives such as C. briggsae share the hermaphrodite-male system, but findings do not automatically generalize across the genus.
sections.conservation: It is not assessed as threatened wildlife; laboratory strains dominate research while natural populations are patchy and hard to find.
